title: How Fabric Capacity Smoothing and Throttling Actually Work
purpose: Trace one operation's Capacity Unit cost from submission through bursting, smoothing, and the four-stage throttling ladder, showing why a sustained overage escalates from invisible to rejected.
accessibleSummary: A flow diagram: an operation is submitted and classified as interactive or background, then allowed to burst above its SKU's steady-state CU rate so it finishes quickly. The bursted cost is smoothed by spreading it across future 30-second timepoints — 5 to 64 minutes for interactive operations, 24 hours for background ones. If accumulated future usage stays under 10 minutes, nothing is throttled. Beyond that, usage escalates through three progressively worse stages: delayed interactive operations, then rejected interactive operations, then rejected background operations too, with carryforward CUs draining only when idle capacity exists at later timepoints. A warning node covers Autoscale Billing for Spark bypassing bursting and smoothing entirely, and a second warning covers Block Public Internet Access breaking Direct Lake regardless of throttling state.
longDescription: This flow starts at operation submission and ends at one of four outcomes on the throttling ladder. Fabric classifies every operation as interactive or background at submission time (before it has actually run), lets it burst above the SKU's steady-state CU allowance so it completes quickly, then smooths that bursted cost across future timepoints — a fixed 30-second unit, 2,880 per day — rather than charging it all at once. Smoothing changes accounting, not wall-clock time: the operation still finishes at normal speed. What smoothing produces is a growing pool of future-committed CU. As long as that future commitment stays under a 10-minute overage-protection window, nothing is throttled. Past that, Fabric escalates in three further stages keyed to how much future capacity is consumed: interactive operations are delayed, then interactive operations are rejected outright, then background operations are rejected too. Carryforward CUs recorded during throttling drain only at timepoints where idle capacity exists, and operations already in flight are always allowed to finish regardless of stage. Two warning nodes cover real traps: Autoscale Billing for Spark removes bursting and smoothing entirely in favor of flat pay-as-you-go metering, and Block Public Internet Access breaks Direct Lake connections independent of any throttling state, which teams sizing a capacity for Direct Lake sometimes miss.

nodes.label: Operation submitted to capacity
nodes.summary: Every workload draws Capacity Units from one dedicated resource pool.
nodes.detail: A capacity is a dedicated pool of resources that performs work in Fabric; capacity units (CUs) are the single unit of compute measurement, and every workload and operation submitted against that capacity draws CUs from its available pool. Throttling is enforced at the capacity level, not the tenant level, so a saturated capacity only affects the workspaces assigned to it — other capacities keep operating normally.
nodes.whyItMatters: Because enforcement is per-capacity, the blast radius of a busy workload is a design lever: isolating a noisy pipeline on its own capacity protects everything else on the tenant.

evidence.note: A capacity is a dedicated pool of resources that performs work in Fabric; capacity units (CUs) are the single unit of compute measurement, drawn from the available pool by every workload and operation.
Fabric enforces throttling at the capacity level rather than the tenant level, so a saturated capacity only affects the workspaces assigned to it.

inputs: A user or scheduled action: a report query, a pipeline run, a Spark job, a semantic model refresh
processing: Operation is attributed to the workspace's assigned capacity
CU cost begins accruing against that capacity's pool
drill.example: A scheduled semantic model refresh on Workspace A (capacity C1) begins consuming CUs from C1 only; Workspace B on capacity C2 sees no effect even if C1 is saturated.
controls: Which capacity a workspace is assigned to
SKU size, which sets the steady-state CU pool
failureModes: Assigning many unrelated high-load workspaces to one capacity, concentrating throttling risk that per-capacity isolation was meant to avoid

nodes.label: Classify: interactive vs background
nodes.summary: Fabric classifies the operation before it runs, which sets its smoothing window.
nodes.detail: The throttling system classifies operations at submission time, before execution begins, so classification can change once runtime information becomes available; in ambiguous cases the system defaults toward the more conservative classification. This classification determines everything downstream: interactive operations get a short smoothing window, background operations get a full day.
nodes.whyItMatters: The classification is what makes a report query behave differently from a pipeline run under load — it is the fork that decides how quickly an operation's cost gets absorbed versus deferred.

evidence.note: The throttling system classifies operations at submission time before execution begins, so classification can change once runtime information becomes available; ambiguous cases default toward the conservative classification.

inputs: The submitted operation and its declared/inferred type
processing: Determine interactive (DAX query, report view, on-demand refresh) vs background (scheduled refresh, pipeline, Spark batch job)
Default to the conservative classification when ambiguous
outputs: An interactive or background label that sets the smoothing window used downstream
drill.example: A user opening a Power BI report is classified interactive; the same report's overnight scheduled refresh is classified background, even though both eventually touch the same semantic model.
controls: No direct admin control over classification; it follows from the operation type itself
failureModes: Assuming a mixed workload is uniformly interactive, then being surprised when its background component smooths over 24 hours instead of minutes

nodes.label: Bursting
nodes.summary: The operation is allowed to consume more CUs than steady-state SKU size allows, to finish quickly.
nodes.detail: Fabric uses two complementary mechanisms: bursting lets an operation consume more CUs than the SKU's steady-state provision allows, so it completes quickly, and smoothing spreads that consumed CU cost across future timepoints rather than charging it all in the moment. Bursting is what happens first, at execution time; smoothing is the accounting mechanism that follows.
nodes.whyItMatters: Bursting is why a spike in demand doesn't immediately slow down the operation itself — the cost of the spike is deferred, not the operation.

evidence.note: Fabric uses two complementary mechanisms — bursting (letting an operation consume more CUs than the SKU provision allows so it completes quickly) and smoothing (spreading that consumed CU cost across future timepoints).

inputs: A classified operation whose demand exceeds the SKU's steady-state CU rate
processing: Allow the operation to draw above the steady-state CU allowance
Complete execution at normal wall-clock speed
outputs: A completed operation and a bursted CU cost handed to smoothing for accounting
drill.example: A large ad-hoc DAX query on an F64 briefly draws well above F64's steady-state CU rate to return in a couple of seconds instead of stalling — the accounting for that extra draw is deferred to smoothing.
controls: No admin toggle for bursting itself; it applies automatically unless Autoscale Billing for Spark is enabled (see the warning node)
failureModes: Reading 'no visible slowdown' as 'no cost' — the bursted CU cost still has to be paid back through smoothing

nodes.label: Smoothing (30-second timepoints)
nodes.summary: Bursted CU cost is spread across future timepoints instead of charged all at once.
nodes.detail: A Fabric timepoint is 30 seconds long, with 2,880 timepoints in a 24-hour window; smoothing distributes an operation's CU cost across those future timepoints rather than charging the full amount immediately. Interactive operations are smoothed over a minimum of 5 minutes and up to 64 minutes depending on total CU consumption, while background operations are always smoothed over a full 24-hour window.
nodes.whyItMatters: Smoothing only changes how CU consumption is accounted for over the window, not the wall-clock execution time of the operation — the query still finishes fast; what smoothing manages is the future capacity commitment that determines whether throttling kicks in next.

evidence.note: A Fabric timepoint is 30 seconds long, with 2,880 timepoints in a 24-hour window; smoothing distributes an operation's CU cost across future timepoints.
Interactive operations are smoothed over a minimum of 5 minutes and up to 64 minutes depending on total CU consumption; background operations are always smoothed over a full 24-hour window.
Smoothing only changes how Capacity Unit consumption is accounted for over the smoothing window, not the wall-clock execution time of the underlying operation.

processing: Spread the CU cost across 30-second timepoints out to 5–64 minutes (interactive) or 24 hours (background)
Accumulate the spread cost into the capacity's future-usage ledger
outputs: A future-usage commitment that the overage-protection window checks next
drill.example: A background pipeline job's burst cost is spread evenly across the next 24 hours of 30-second timepoints, so its accounting impact on any single timepoint is small even though the job itself finished in minutes.
controls: No direct admin control over the smoothing window length; it follows from the interactive/background classification and total CU consumed
failureModes: Not realizing that many smoothed operations stacking on the same future timepoints is what eventually triggers throttling, even though each individual operation looked fine in isolation

nodes.label: Overage-protection check (10-minute window)
nodes.summary: The decision point: is accumulated future usage under or over the 10-minute threshold?
nodes.detail: Throttling is staged progressively across four thresholds keyed to how much future capacity has been consumed: up to 10 minutes of future usage triggers no throttling at all (overage protection). Past that window, Fabric moves through three further stages of increasing severity. This is the branch point in the ladder — everything before it is invisible to users; everything after it is not.
nodes.whyItMatters: This threshold is the line between a capacity that looks completely normal and one that starts visibly delaying or rejecting work — understanding it is what turns capacity monitoring from guesswork into a leading indicator.

evidence.note: Throttling is staged progressively across four thresholds keyed to how much future capacity has been consumed: up to 10 minutes of future usage triggers no throttling (overage protection).

inputs: The capacity's accumulated future-usage ledger from smoothing
processing: Compare accumulated future CU commitment against the 10-minute overage-protection threshold
Route to no-throttling or to the escalating stages based on the result
outputs: A throttling stage decision applied to new operation submissions
drill.example: A capacity with three concurrent heavy background jobs accumulates 14 minutes of future usage, crossing the 10-minute threshold and entering the first throttling stage for any new interactive request.
controls: Reducing concurrent load, rescheduling background jobs off-peak, or scaling the SKU before the threshold is crossed
failureModes: Monitoring only current CPU/CU usage and missing that the future-usage ledger, not current load, is what determines throttling

nodes.label: No throttling
nodes.summary: Under the 10-minute overage window: operations proceed normally with no visible impact.
nodes.detail: When accumulated future-capacity usage stays within the 10-minute overage-protection window, no throttling is applied at all. This is the steady state for a well-sized capacity most of the time.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is the outcome a correctly sized capacity should live in almost always — seeing it escalate past this stage regularly is the signal that the SKU or workload distribution needs attention.

evidence.note: Up to 10 minutes of future usage triggers no throttling (overage protection).

inputs: An overage-protection check result under 10 minutes of future usage
processing: No delay or rejection applied
New operations submit and execute normally
drill.example: A steady daytime workload of report queries and small scheduled refreshes keeps future usage around 3–4 minutes on an F64, never approaching the threshold.
controls: Right-sizing the SKU to average sustained load, per Microsoft's own capacity-optimization guidance
failureModes: Sizing for this comfortable steady state without headroom for real bursts, so a single busy month-end pushes straight past it

nodes.label: Stage 2: interactive delay
nodes.summary: Between 10 minutes and further thresholds: new interactive operations are delayed, not rejected.
nodes.detail: Past the 10-minute overage-protection window, the first escalation stage delays new interactive operation submissions rather than rejecting them outright. Operations already in flight when a capacity enters a throttling state are always allowed to run to completion — only new submissions are subject to delay or rejection at any stage.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is usually the first sign users notice: reports feel sluggish to open, but nothing fails outright yet — a warning stage, not a hard failure.

evidence.note: Throttling is staged progressively; between the overage-protection window and further thresholds, new interactive operations are delayed.
Operations that were already in flight when a capacity enters a throttling state are always allowed to run to completion; only new operation submissions are subject to delay or rejection.

inputs: An overage-protection check result past the 10-minute threshold, first escalation band
processing: New interactive operation submissions are held before executing
In-flight operations continue unaffected
drill.example: A user opening a report during a month-end batch surge experiences a multi-second delay before the visuals render, while the batch job that was already running finishes on schedule.
failureModes: Dismissing delayed-but-successful queries as 'just slow today' instead of reading them as an early throttling signal

nodes.label: Stage 3: interactive rejection
nodes.summary: Further past threshold: new interactive requests are rejected with CapacityLimitExceeded.
nodes.detail: As accumulated future usage grows further past the overage-protection window, Fabric escalates to rejecting new interactive operation submissions. When a capacity rejects requests, users receive HTTP status code CapacityLimitExceeded along with error messages indicating that compute capacity limits have been reached.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is the stage where users start seeing visible errors instead of slowness — the point at which throttling stops being a performance annoyance and becomes an outage for interactive work.

evidence.note: When a capacity rejects requests, users receive HTTP status code CapacityLimitExceeded along with error messages indicating that compute capacity limits have been reached.

inputs: Future usage escalated well past the overage-protection window with no relief
processing: New interactive submissions are rejected at the API level
In-flight operations still run to completion
outputs: CapacityLimitExceeded errors surfaced to users attempting new interactive actions
drill.example: During a sustained overload, a user opening a new report gets a CapacityLimitExceeded error while an already-open report's visuals, mid-render before the stage escalated, still complete.
controls: Pausing non-critical background jobs to let carryforward CUs drain
failureModes: No alerting on the delay stage means this rejection stage is the first anyone notices a problem, well after the leading indicator was available

nodes.label: Stage 4: background rejection too
nodes.summary: Worst stage: background operations are rejected as well, in addition to interactive ones.
nodes.detail: The final and most severe throttling stage rejects new background operation submissions in addition to interactive ones. Carryforward CUs recorded during throttling drain at each subsequent timepoint that has idle capacity, so recovery from this stage depends on demand actually easing rather than any manual reset.
nodes.whyItMatters: At this stage nothing new can start on the capacity — it is the clearest signal that the SKU is undersized for its workload, not just experiencing a transient spike.

evidence.note: Throttling escalates through further thresholds until background operations are rejected in addition to interactive ones.
When accumulated future-capacity usage exceeds the overage protection window, the excess is recorded as carryforward CUs; each subsequent timepoint with idle capacity reduces this carryforward.

inputs: Sustained accumulated future usage that never eased through the delay or interactive-rejection stages
processing: New background submissions rejected alongside interactive ones
Carryforward CU balance drains only at timepoints with idle capacity
outputs: A capacity that accepts no new work of either kind until carryforward drains
drill.example: A capacity running a multi-hour Spark backfill alongside heavy report traffic hits stage 4; new pipeline triggers and new report opens both fail until the backfill finishes and carryforward CUs drain over subsequent idle timepoints.
controls: Splitting the offending workload onto a separate capacity
Scaling the SKU up before recurring peak windows
failureModes: Treating this as a bug to retry through, when the actual fix is reducing load or increasing capacity so carryforward can drain

nodes.label: Burndown and carryforward drain
nodes.summary: Carryforward CUs recorded during throttling drain only at timepoints with idle capacity.
nodes.detail: When accumulated future usage exceeds the overage protection window, excess compute is recorded as carryforward CUs. At each future 30-second timepoint where the capacity is not fully utilized, unconsumed capacity is applied to burn down this carryforward balance until it reaches zero.
nodes.whyItMatters: A capacity cannot recover from throttling until carryforward CUs are completely drained; simply stopping new queries is not enough if background jobs keep utilizing available timepoints.

evidence.note: When accumulated future-capacity usage exceeds the overage protection window, the excess is recorded as carryforward CUs; each subsequent timepoint with idle capacity reduces this carryforward.

inputs: Carryforward CU balance accumulated from stages 2, 3, or 4
processing: Evaluate available idle CUs at each subsequent 30s timepoint
Deduct idle CUs from the carryforward ledger until balance reaches zero
outputs: Recovery from throttled state back to normal Stage 1 operations
drill.example: An overnight batch job generates 45 minutes of carryforward debt; during morning quiet hours, 50% idle capacity on each 30s timepoint drains the carryforward balance over the next 90 minutes.
controls: Scaling SKU size up to increase idle CU burndown rate
failureModes: Continuing to run back-to-back heavy jobs with zero idle timepoints, preventing carryforward from draining and extending throttling indefinitely

nodes.label: Autoscale Billing for Spark bypasses this entirely
nodes.summary: When enabled, Spark drops bursting and smoothing for flat pay-as-you-go metering.
nodes.detail: Bursting and smoothing do not apply when a capacity admin has enabled Autoscale Billing for Spark; in that configuration Spark usage operates in pay-as-you-go mode only, metered separately from the standard capacity's smoothing ladder.
nodes.whyItMatters: A team that assumes all Spark load shares the same throttling ladder as everything else on the capacity will misdiagnose Spark cost and contention once Autoscale Billing is turned on — it is a genuinely separate metering path, not a variant of the same one.

evidence.note: Bursting and smoothing do not apply when a capacity admin has enabled Autoscale Billing for Spark; in that configuration Spark usage operates in pay-as-you-go mode only.

inputs: A capacity with Autoscale Billing for Spark enabled by an admin
processing: Spark jobs are metered as pay-as-you-go compute, independent of the capacity's bursting/smoothing ledger
outputs: Spark cost and contention that never appears in the throttling stages diagrammed above
drill.example: A capacity shows no throttling stage escalation despite heavy concurrent Spark notebooks, because Autoscale Billing routes that Spark usage around the smoothing ladder entirely — the cost shows up as separate pay-as-you-go billing instead.
controls: Deciding per capacity whether Autoscale Billing for Spark is worth trading smoothing protection for predictable per-job billing
failureModes: Assuming Spark contention will show up as capacity throttling like everything else, and missing a real cost/performance signal because it is routed elsewhere

nodes.label: Block Public Internet Access breaks Direct Lake regardless
nodes.summary: A network-isolation setting, not throttling, that silently forces Direct Lake off public endpoints.
nodes.detail: Direct Lake connections fail when the Block Public Internet Access tenant setting is active, because semantic models relying on Direct Lake mode must route through public endpoints — a constraint that applies independent of any throttling stage on the capacity itself.
nodes.whyItMatters: Teams sizing a capacity purely against the throttling ladder can miss that a separate, unrelated tenant network setting can break Direct Lake outright — the failure looks capacity-related but isn't.

evidence.note: Direct Lake connections fail when the Block Public Internet Access tenant setting is active. Semantic models relying on Direct Lake mode must route through public endpoints.

inputs: A tenant with Block Public Internet Access enabled
Semantic models configured for Direct Lake
processing: Direct Lake attempts to route through the public endpoint that is now blocked
Connection fails, independent of the capacity's CU or throttling state
outputs: Direct Lake models that fail to connect even on an otherwise healthy, unthrottled capacity
drill.example: A capacity shows no throttling and plenty of headroom, yet Direct Lake reports fail to load after a tenant admin enables Block Public Internet Access for network isolation — the two problems are unrelated but easy to conflate during troubleshooting.
controls: Evaluate private-link and network-isolation settings and Direct Lake dependency together before enabling Block Public Internet Access
failureModes: Diagnosing a Direct Lake outage as a capacity or throttling problem and scaling the SKU, when the actual cause is a network setting

edges.label: carryforward CUs drain at idle timepoints
bypassed if Autoscale Billing for Spark is on
independent risk: network isolation, not load

walkthrough.title: Start: an operation draws CUs from one capacity
walkthrough.explanation: Throttling is enforced per capacity, so understanding one capacity's ladder is enough to reason about the blast radius of any workload assigned to it.

walkthrough.title: Classification sets the smoothing window
walkthrough.explanation: Interactive vs background is decided at submission time and determines whether the operation smooths over minutes or a full day.

walkthrough.title: Bursting lets the operation finish fast
walkthrough.explanation: The operation can draw above the SKU's steady-state CU rate so it completes quickly — the cost of that overage is deferred, not avoided.

walkthrough.title: Smoothing spreads the deferred cost
walkthrough.explanation: The bursted cost is spread across 30-second timepoints — 5 to 64 minutes for interactive work, a full day for background work.

walkthrough.title: The 10-minute decision point
walkthrough.explanation: This is the branch: under 10 minutes of accumulated future usage, nothing is throttled; past it, escalation begins.

walkthrough.title: The steady state most capacities should live in
walkthrough.explanation: No visible impact — this is where a correctly sized capacity spends most of its time.

walkthrough.title: First escalation: interactive operations slow down
walkthrough.explanation: New interactive requests are delayed, not rejected — the first user-visible sign of pressure.

walkthrough.title: Second escalation: interactive requests fail outright
walkthrough.explanation: New interactive submissions now return CapacityLimitExceeded, though anything already running still completes.

walkthrough.title: Worst case: nothing new can start
walkthrough.explanation: Background submissions are rejected too; recovery depends on carryforward CUs draining at future idle timepoints, not a manual reset.

walkthrough.title: Burndown: excess debt drains at idle timepoints
walkthrough.explanation: Accumulated carryforward CUs are reduced at each future 30-second timepoint with idle capacity until the balance drains to zero.

walkthrough.title: Warning: Spark can opt out of this whole ladder
walkthrough.explanation: Autoscale Billing for Spark routes Spark usage to flat pay-as-you-go metering, bypassing bursting and smoothing entirely — a separate cost and contention path.

walkthrough.title: Warning: a network setting can look like a capacity problem
walkthrough.explanation: Block Public Internet Access breaks Direct Lake independent of throttling — an easy misdiagnosis during an outage.
